summary:
**INFINITUM — Lunar Landing Site Navigator**

Choosing a lunar landing site is not simply about finding a suitable place on the Moon; it is about understanding how the surrounding terrain shapes the conditions a future mission will experience. A nearby ridge can block sunlight, reduce potential solar energy, or obstruct direct visibility of Earth—even when the astronomical geometry appears favorable.

**INFINITUM** addresses this challenge through a terrain-aware analysis platform that combines lunar elevation data with astronomical ephemerides from NASA/JPL Horizons. Focusing on seven candidate regions within Site 01 – Connecting Ridge, it evaluates terrain-obstructed solar illumination, estimates ideal and terrain-adjusted solar power and energy, analyzes Earth's geometric visibility, and identifies illumination and visibility windows over time. It also provides a weighted comparison of the selected locations.

By bringing terrain, sunlight, energy potential, and Earth visibility into one interactive environment, INFINITUM transforms complex scientific data into insights that are easier to explore and compare. Its goal is to help mission planners understand not just what a lunar location looks like, but how its landscape may shape the opportunities and constraints of operating there.
details:
INFINITUM – Lunar Landing Site Navigator

INFINITUM is a terrain-aware analysis platform designed to help explore how the lunar landscape influences the operating conditions of potential landing locations. Focusing on seven candidate regions (ROIs) within Site 01 – Connecting Ridge, it combines lunar elevation data with astronomical calculations from NASA/JPL Horizons to analyze sunlight availability, potential solar energy, and Earth's geometric visibility over time.

The platform evaluates the Sun's position relative to the local terrain horizon, calculates the visible fraction of the solar disk, and estimates both ideal and terrain-adjusted solar power and energy. It also analyzes Earth's geometric visibility and identifies illumination and visibility windows, allowing users to examine how conditions change with location and time. A comparison system brings these factors together to help users explore differences between the selected regions.

One important insight from our analysis is that two nearby locations can experience very different sunlight conditions because of surrounding terrain. For example, during the tested period, the solar disk was obstructed at ROI 1, resulting in zero terrain-adjusted solar power, while ROI 2 had full solar-disk visibility and reached a maximum estimated terrain-adjusted power of 8.410 W under our model assumptions.

INFINITUM's main benefit is bringing terrain, astronomical geometry, solar-energy estimation, and Earth visibility analysis into one interactive environment instead of requiring users to interpret separate datasets and tools. Its intended impact is to support early-stage lunar site assessment and help mission planners better understand potential environmental opportunities and constraints.

The project was developed using Python in Google Colab, with libraries and tools including NumPy, Pandas, Requests, Gradio, and geospatial data-processing tools. We used lunar Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data, ROI geographic data, and NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides. The interactive Mission Control interface allows users to select a candidate region and a date and time to explore the corresponding analysis.

What makes INFINITUM creative is its terrain-aware approach: it goes beyond astronomical position alone and examines whether the surrounding lunar landscape actually allows sunlight or geometric visibility. We considered location, time, terrain obstruction, solar-disk visibility, energy-model assumptions, and the limitations of geometric Earth visibility. The resulting platform turns complex scientific data into a more accessible and comparable set of mission-relevant insights.
